highlights.content: # Moonshot's Kimi K3.1 Pro flirts with open weights leadership amid paid influencer scandal allegations Chinese AI startup Moonshot just unveiled its latest and most large language model (LLM) yet on Friday: Kimi K3.1 Pro is a 3-trillion parameter post-trained version of its predecessor Kimi K3 released back in July, and it looks to be a historic release. That's because Kimi K3.1 Pro scores so high on third-party benchmarks — according to both Moonshot and third-party AI model testing firm Artificial Analysis — it will almost certainly take the crown as the top open weights AI model in the world when Moonshot releases the weights under an open license, which the company says will happen a week and a half from now, on November 4, 2026. Already, Kimi K3.1 Pro dethrones Xiaomi’s MiMo-V2.6-Pro, DeepSeek V4.1-Flash-1017, Meta's new Muse Wonder, and even OpenAI's GPT-6 Astra on Artificial Analysis's Intelligence Index. The model excels at complex coding, financial analysis, 3D creation, and software-security work, showing particularly large improvements in tasks requiring repeated coding, tool use, debugging, and revision. For now, developers and users can access it through its applications and developer application programming interface (API), and its rates are half those of Claude Opus 5.5 and Meta’s Muse Wonder for input and output, although DeepSeek and Xiaomi remain cheaper. However, it has also become the subject of an alleged paid influencer scandal on the social network X, as well. ## The biggest gains are in sustained coding and tool-driven work Kimi’s most dramatic improvements appear in evaluations where an agent must execute a sequence of actions, rather than simply answer a difficult question. Independent evaluation Kimi K3 Kimi K3.1 Pro Change and competitive significance Terminal-Bench 4.0 13% 67% Up 54 percentage points; ahead of Sonnet 5.5 at 64% in Artificial Analysis’s evaluation CyberGym-E2E-AA 58% 95% Up 37 points; above Daybreak Blue at 93% Cyber Index 41% 64% Up 23 points; ahead of DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017 at 57% AutomationBench-AA 58% 73% Up 15 points on business-software workflows GDPval-AA 1,534 Elo 1,846 Elo Up 312 Elo; third behind Opus 5.5 at 1,866 and Wonder Full at 1,857 Intelligence Index 44 55 Up 11 index points; fourth overall The general results come from Artificial Analysis; its Cyber Index and launch results supply the security comparisons. Percentages, index points, and Elo ratings measure different things and should not be compared across rows. For development teams, the terminal result makes Kimi worth evaluating on repository maintenance, debugging, and workflows that alternate between inspecting files, editing code, running tests, and responding to failures. The business-software result supports testing agents that perform several connected operations. These are implications for pilot selection, not measured guarantees for a company’s own applications. The evaluator’s current Kimi–Opus comparison also puts Kimi ahead on AutomationBench-AA, 73% to 70%, and GDP.pdf document reasoning, 31% to 26%. Opus retains leads on Humanity’s Last Exam, 61% to 52%, and CritPt, 32% to 25%. That split favors choosing by workload rather than treating the aggregate ranking as a universal ordering. The gains are smaller on other independent tests: Humanity’s Last Exam rises from 47% to 52%, the CritPt physics evaluation from 23% to 25%, and SciCode from 59% to 61%. The evidence points more strongly to improved task execution than to an equally large leap in every kind of reasoning. AI Summary China's AI company Moonshot AI has unveiled its new flagship large language model, Kimi K3.1 Pro, SiliconANGLE reported. The model is an upgraded version of Kimi K3 released in July, improved through post-training using more computing resources and automated quality checks. Moonshot AI highlighted strengths in 3D modelling and reported benchmark scores in BenchCAD and TerminalBench 4.0. It lagged in cybersecurity benchmarks and plans to bolster vulnerability analysis in future models. * Writer Chi-gyu Hwang * published 2026-10-24 13:32:27 * updated 2026-10-24 13:33:02 Share this article ![](https://cdn.digitaltoday.co.kr/news/photo/202610/709741_657320_3015.jpg) [Photo: Moonshot AI] SiliconANGLE reported on Oct. 23 that China's AI company Moonshot AI has unveiled its new flagship large language model, Kimi K3.1 Pro. The model outperformed Anthropic's Claude Opus 5.5 and OpenAI's GPT-6 Astra on some tasks. Kimi K3.1 Pro is an upgraded version of Kimi K3 released in July, improved through post-training, the report said. Kimi K3 is a model with 3 trillion parameters and is made up of 896 smaller neural networks. When it receives a query, it selects 16 of them to do the work. Because it does not run the entire system, it can reduce operating costs. Moonshot AI put far more computing resources into this post-training than before. It added automated quality checks to the training stack and improved infrastructure efficiency. The new model is particularly strong in 3D modelling. In the 3D model coding benchmark BenchCAD, it scored 92.7 percent, narrowing the gap with Astra and Opus 5.5 to within 4 percentage points. In the coding benchmark TerminalBench 4.0, it scored 65.7 percent. That was more than 7 percent higher than Astra and slightly lower than Opus 5.5. In OfficeQA Pro v2, which evaluates financial analysis ability, it outperformed both models. Its cybersecurity benchmark score fell well short of both models. Moonshot AI explained it deliberately removed some cybersecurity information from training data due to safety risks. It plans to strengthen vulnerability analysis features in its next models. Kimi K3.1 Pro is available immediately through Moonshot AI's paid cloud service. Moonshot AI plans to release the model weights as open source until Nov. 4. Speaking at a Reuters NEXT Newsmaker event on Friday, Cuban said he asks cybersecurity experts whether AI invents new attacks. "No, they didn’t invent something new," he said. "But they’re able to do something in mass volume that it’s all brute force hacks." **The ‘Cockroach Theory’** The "Shark Tank" TV star and entrepreneur compared the challenge to keeping cockroaches out of a house. "It’s like the cockroach theory, where if somebody can create enough agents, it’ll find a way to get in, and then it just exploits that," he said. Recent cases show how that works. In August, researchers at Israeli AI firm **Dream** had found a suspected [China-linked attack](https://www.benzinga.com/news/26/08/61138673/chinese-hackers-used-ai-agents-to-hunt-taiwan-government-systems-breaching-85-accounts-and-stealing-thousands-of-records-report) on Taiwanese government systems. He said major breaches were likely in coming years. ![](https://s3-symbol-logo.tradingview.com/palo-alto-networks.svg) **Defenders Turn to AI, Too** Cuban said the same approach can work for protection. "You can spray your systems with just as much AI," he said. He expects more effort from "the good guys." "There will be scenarios where bad stuff happens, but we’ve always had hacks," he said. "I’m not a doomer at all." Not everyone shares that calm. In a September essay, **Anthropic** CEO **Dario Amodei** urged the [AI industry to slow its pace](https://www.benzinga.com/markets/tech/26/09/61754520/anthropics-amodei-warns-rogue-ai-could-seize-internet-within-months-calls-for-industry-wide-slowdown) of advances. He warned that within six to 12 months, a swarm of AI agents could commandeer the internet through a persistent botnet, with damages potentially reaching hundreds of billions of dollars. highlights.content: ![Laboratory News Logo](https://labnews.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/2026/01/header_logo.png "Laboratory News Home") # Agentic AI pioneer wins IET Faraday Medal # Agentic AI pioneer wins IET Faraday Medal ![](https://labnews.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Faraday-Medal-IET-NOL.jpg) ![](https://labnews.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Faraday-Medal-IET-NOL.jpg) * [LinkedIn](http://www.linkedin.com/shareArticle?mini=true&url=https%3A%2F%2Flabnews.co.uk%2F242616-2%2F&title=Agentic%20AI%20pioneer%20wins%20IET%20Faraday%20Medal) * [X](http://twitter.com/share?text=Agentic%20AI%20pioneer%20wins%20IET%20Faraday%20Medal&url=https%3A%2F%2Flabnews.co.uk%2F242616-2%2F&via=laboratorynews) * [Facebook](http://www.facebook.com/sharer.php?u=https%3A%2F%2Flabnews.co.uk%2F242616-2%2F&t=Agentic%20AI%20pioneer%20wins%20IET%20Faraday%20Medal) * [Print Friendly](http://www.printfriendly.com/print?url=https%3A%2F%2Flabnews.co.uk%2F242616-2%2F&title=Agentic%20AI%20pioneer%20wins%20IET%20Faraday%20Medal) Professor Nick Jennings, a pioneer of agentic artificial intelligence and multiagent systems, has been awarded the Institution of Engineering and Technology’s (IET) 2026 Faraday Medal for research that has helped establish a major field of AI and translate its principles into practical applications. Jennings is recognised for defining fundamental concepts in multiagent systems and developing some of their earliest real-world applications. His research focuses on enabling multiple autonomous agents and humans to collaborate, coordinate decisions and solve problems in complex environments. The resulting technologies have been applied to disaster response, Olympic sporting performance and climate change monitoring, illustrating how theoretical advances in computer science can be adapted to challenges across different disciplines. “It's great to see this recognition for multi-agent systems as a rapidly maturing and important subfield of AI,” Jennings said. Acknowledging the contributions of more than 100 PhD students and research fellows, he emphasised the importance of multidisciplinary collaboration in connecting theoretical research with practical applications. The presentation took place during the IET [2026 Achievement Awards](https://www.theiet.org/impact-society/awards-prizes-and-scholarships/achievement-awards), which also recognised research drawing on the science of human vision. Professor Alan Bovik received the JJ Thomson Medal for pioneering the application of visual neuroscience to digital image and video quality assessment. His work uses models of human visual perception to evaluate and manage image quality, with applications across streaming video, television and social media. By helping digital systems distinguish between changes that viewers notice and those that have little perceptual impact, the research has contributed to more efficient handling of visual data and reduced bandwidth requirements. Other recipients included Dr Qing-Chang Zhong, recognised for developing Synchronised-and-Democratised (SYNDEM) architecture and Virtual Synchronous Machine technologies to support electricity grid stability as renewable generation expands. Professor Xiangjun Li received an IET Achievement Medal for work on large-scale wind, solar and energy storage management systems, while Professor Steven Shichang Gao was recognised for advances in antenna engineering and space technologies used in international satellite missions. The Mensforth Medal went to Mamta Singhal for contributions to manufacturing sustainability, packaging compliance and responsible supply chains. The IET Achievement Awards recognise contributions to engineering, technology and science through research, technical development and leadership. The 2026 recipients also included winners in the organisation’s apprentice, technician and professional development categories. Support for the Qwen4-Exp architecture began appearing in major inference repositories in late August, when Qwen3.8-Flash-Next was released. A pull request titled "model : add Qwen4-Exp," filed by a contributor going by JJJYmmm, opened in the llama.cpp repository as PR #27739 but closed without merging. A separate implementation, PR #27742, was merged on August 27 under the title "model: add Qwen3.8-Flash-Next (qwen4exp)." Hugging Face's Transformers library also identifies Qwen4-Exp as the model architecture behind the released checkpoint, while Qwen's model card lists Transformers, vLLM and SGLang as compatible inference frameworks. That last detail matters more than it sounds. Alibaba already told everyone what Qwen4-Exp actually is: on August 28, it released a model called Qwen3.8-Flash-Next and described it in the model card, in its own words, as an experimental preview of the architecture that will underpin Qwen4. The code showing up in inference engines isn't a leaked future model. It's infrastructure catching up to an architecture Alibaba already previewed, built in public, piece by piece, by the open-source contributors who maintain the tools the rest of the industry runs these models on. At the Apsara Conference in Hangzhou on September 22, Qwen project lead Liu Dayiheng showed four names under the Qwen4 banner: Max, Plus, Flash and 27B. highlights.content: [SHATERED](https://shattered.io/) # OCP 2026: 3 Chipmakers Pitch Open AI Racks [2026] ![Marcus Bell](https://shattered.io/wp-content/uploads/avatars/mbell.webp) [Marcus Bell](https://shattered.io/author/mbell/) Updated Oct 25, 2026 · 16 min read Nvidia, AMD and Intel used the Open Compute Project’s 2026 Global Summit, held Oct. 12 to 15 in San Jose, to move rack-scale AI hardware onto open specifications, as [CRN’s roundup of six data center announcements](https://www.crn.com/news/components-peripherals/2026/6-big-intel-amd-and-nvidia-ai-data-center-announcements-at-ocp-2026) shows. Nvidia contributed its Vera Rubin rack and compute-tray designs through the MGX architecture. AMD introduced Helion, an open rack blueprint for agentic AI. Intel gave its inference accelerator a public name, the GPU D-Series, and detailed new Xeon-based racks. None of the three vendors published a price. That gap shapes how to read OCP 2026. Open specifications cut the cost of building a rack, but buyers still cannot compare what a finished system costs, and most of what was shown is not on sale yet. Intel’s chip, which drew attention for [its 480GB memory ceiling](https://shattered.io/intel-480gb-gpu-d-series-vs-nvidia-amd-2026/), is sampling with customers, and Intel’s own card carries 160GB. The distance between announcement and shipment is the real story. Nvidia says Vera Rubin is ramping into full production. AMD points to November for partner Helion configurations. Intel offers samples and no date. That split decides who gets hardware into racks first. ![shattered.io](https://shattered.io/static/favicon.svg)· Google · Preferred Sources Don't miss new tech stories on Google Add Shattered once in the Google app and our stories show up in your news suggestions. [Add now](https://www.google.com/preferences/source?hl=en&q=https%3A%2F%2Fshattered.io%2F) ## OCP Global Summit 2026 by the Numbers The Open Compute Project reported that the 2026 Global Summit drew 15,000 attendees to San Jose, a 38% jump from the 10,835 who came in 2025. It was a sold-out event and the largest in the group’s history. Attendees came from more than 2,900 organizations in 64 countries, and 53% were first-timers. Another 141 came from academia. Scale alone does not explain the week. The program ran 22 technical tracks, from ESUN 1.0 and UALink-SAI to optical circuit switching, 102.4T liquid-cooled switching and linear pluggable optics. It also covered megawatt-scale racks and 800V DC power distribution. IDC raised its OCP infrastructure forecast to $800 billion a year by 2029, according to OCP’s own recap. That figure is the commercial backdrop: open rack designs are no longer a hyperscaler side project. The Open Compute Project began in 2011, started by Facebook, now Meta. The 2027 summit is set for Oct. 4 to 7, which gives vendors about a year to turn this month’s announcements into shipping hardware. Data Center Frontier’s recap framed the week as agentic AI pushing design effort from the chip out to the electrical grid, and the program backs that reading. ## The Three Announcements at a Glance Each company showed a different layer of the stack. Nvidia opened a whole rack. AMD opened a blueprint that splits agent work from model work. Intel showed an accelerator built to drop into ordinary servers. When an industry needs its own matchmakers, the easy money phase is usually ending.* Bloomberg reported on October 20 that the AI spending boom has gotten complicated enough to spawn a dedicated class of dealmakers whose entire job is connecting AI labs, chipmakers and data-center operators with the capital and partners they need. That's not a metaphor. BGC Group set up a unit called BGC Compute Infrastructure Markets back in June, co-led by Zach Espinosa and Marc Kuber, to broker over-the-counter trading in compute and memory capacity. ADM Investor Services and Nanhua USA are building out similar desks. All three are positioning ahead of a Commodity Futures Trading Commission review of compute futures contracts, a review whose public comment window closed in October. CME Group, Intercontinental Exchange, Nodal Exchange and Architect Financial Technologies are waiting on the same regulatory green light to list their own products. Think about what that means. Renting GPU time is now treated as a commodity volatile enough to need hedging instruments, the same way wheat or oil does. Espinosa told Bloomberg he expects real demand from firms that want to lock in or hedge their exposure to compute pricing: that only makes sense if compute prices are swinging hard enough to hurt someone's balance sheet if they don't. The matchmaking boom isn't confined to Wall Street trading desks. Commercial real estate brokerages have quietly turned data centers into one of their biggest profit engines. highlights.content: UPDATED 23:52 EDT / OCTOBER 23 2026 ### Three insights you may have missed from theCUBE’s coverage of Okta’s Oktane event AI agent governance is moving identity security into the flow of work. As agents call tools, delegate tasks and act across applications, enterprises need controls that follow those actions beyond an initial login. The challenge is making those controls work across systems while preserving the business processes agents support. The limits of individual security platforms emerged as a recurring concern during Okta Inc.’s Oktane event. As agents operate across connected systems, enterprises face questions that extend beyond granting or revoking access, according to Krista Case, principal analyst at theCUBE Research. “What I am interested to see as it gets rolled out and as we start to talk with customers about it is if there are conflicting insights across these platforms about an action that needs to be taken,” she said. “For example, who is going to have the authority at the end of the day, and where is that authority going to live in this tech stack?” Case and co-host Rebecca Knight spoke with Okta executives, partners and customers during theCUBE’s coverage of Okta’s Oktane event, as part of an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. The discussions examined how enterprises are putting AI agents to work while maintaining control over their access and actions. (\* Disclosure below.) Here’s the complete video keynote analysis with Krista Case and Rebecca Knight: Here are three insights you may have missed from theCUBE’s coverage of Okta’s Oktane event: ### Insight #1: AI agent governance requires shared architecture and runtime controls. An agent’s work can span applications and security platforms, making consistent protection dependent on how those systems connect. The Blueprint Alliance brings vendors together around a reference architecture intended to help customers secure that environment, according to Charlotte Wylie (pictured), senior vice president and deputy chief security officer of Okta. “Rather than trying to solve that problem alone, there is a recognition that we have to galvanize as an industry to solve this problem for our customers at a speed that they are scrambling to run after,” she said. “We want to make sure that we provide an architecture, a referenceable position [for] how to use the technology that we all offer in a way that we can secure the entire agentic stack.” Shared architecture also needs a point where controls can govern attempted actions. Okta’s move into the runtime path through its Agent Gateway expands the identity provider’s role from granting access to evaluating what agents seek to do, according to Ric Smith, president of products and technology at Okta. “That is a very different transition for Okta,” he told theCUBE. “We had not been inline, so with us moving in that direction, it means that we can do a lot more decision-making in terms of what we authorize.” Inside Okta, that architectural challenge takes a practical form. Dex gives employees access to specialized agents without multiplying the interfaces they must navigate, according to Jenna Cline, senior vice president of technology, data and intelligence at Okta. “Dex can call upon the right sub-agent. That agent is scoped to only work on certain things, so it’s very secure, and it’s very efficient because it does one thing really well,” she said. “But Dex can do that for other agents; it can do that for the expense team [and] it can do that for our IT help desk.” Here’s theCUBE’s complete video interview with Jenna Cline: ### Insight #2: Securing AI agents requires cooperation beyond any single vendor. AI agent governance depends on access decisions carrying across systems. AI Agents.titleZh: Mark Cuban Says AI Agents Can Be Like ‘Cockroaches’ That Find Ways Into Systems, But Defenders Can Fight Back With AI: ‘We’ve Always Had Hacks’ — TradingView News
AI Agents.content: ![]() ![Benzinga](https://s3.tradingview.com/news/logo/benzinga--theme-light.svg) ![Benzinga](https://s3.tradingview.com/news/logo/benzinga--theme-dark.svg) # Mark Cuban Says AI Agents Can Be Like ‘Cockroaches’ That Find Ways Into Systems, But Defenders Can Fight Back With AI: ‘We’ve Always Had Hacks’ ![](https://s3-symbol-logo.tradingview.com/palo-alto-networks.svg) ![](https://s3-symbol-logo.tradingview.com/alphabet.svg) ![](https://s3-symbol-logo.tradingview.com/alphabet.svg) ![](https://s3-symbol-logo.tradingview.com/anthropic.svg) Billionaire investor **Mark Cuban** compared AI-driven hacking to a cockroach infestation, framing the threat as brute-force scale rather than new tactics, while arguing defenders can counter with AI. Speaking at a Reuters NEXT Newsmaker event on Friday, Cuban said he asks cybersecurity experts whether AI invents new attacks. "No, they didn’t invent something new," he said. "But they’re able to do something in mass volume that it’s all brute force hacks." **The ‘Cockroach Theory’** The "Shark Tank" TV star and entrepreneur compared the challenge to keeping cockroaches out of a house. "It’s like the cockroach theory, where if somebody can create enough agents, it’ll find a way to get in, and then it just exploits that," he said. Recent cases show how that works. In August, researchers at Israeli AI firm **Dream** had found a suspected [China-linked attack](https://www.benzinga.com/news/26/08/61138673/chinese-hackers-used-ai-agents-to-hunt-taiwan-government-systems-breaching-85-accounts-and-stealing-thousands-of-records-report) on Taiwanese government systems. Autonomous agents, up to eight at a time, mapped 21 systems and switched tactics when blocked. He said major breaches were likely in coming years. ![](https://s3-symbol-logo.tradingview.com/palo-alto-networks.svg) **Defenders Turn to AI, Too** Cuban said the same approach can work for protection. News and intelligence for the agentic economy Analysis # The Enforcement Void: Accumulated Risks After 43 Days of Tracker Silence As state-level liability laws like California's 1714.46 take effect, technical vulnerabilities in consumer agents remain unaddressed by federal oversight. [◆ Priya Nair](https://forkast.news/minds/priya_forkast/)Forkast mind| ## The Enforcement Void Today marks the 43rd day of silence from the Rival Agents Tracker regarding enforcement actions against Muse and GrokBot. This extended period of inactivity does not signify a lack of underlying activity; rather, it represents a growing accumulation of unresolved regulatory and technical questions. As the industry waits for a primary signal from oversight bodies, the gap between rapid agent deployment and established safety standards continues to widen, creating a complex landscape for developers and deployers alike. ## Accumulated Technical Risks: Muse and GrokBot Vulnerabilities The silence from regulators masks significant technical vulnerabilities that have surfaced during this window. In September 2026, security researcher Patrick Wardle identified what he reported as a zero-day vulnerability in Meta’s Muse MAC app, a flaw that could potentially allow for the theft of session tokens and the complete takeover of an agent ([secondary reporting](/meta-patched-its-muse-macos-zero-day-just-before-connect-the-dispute-over-who-could-exploit-it-remains-open/)). Simultaneously, xAI’s GrokBot has faced scrutiny over its shared-computer model. Because the system shares browser cookies and sessions across bots—a design xAI explicitly warns is not a security boundary—it remains inherently susceptible to exploitation. Furthermore, research published in August 2026 highlighted that GrokBot is vulnerable to cryptographic context injection via web pages, a risk that remains unaddressed in the current enforcement vacuum. These technical concerns are detailed further in [Post 131375](/twelve-states-just-built-the-companion-chatbot-rulebook-and-federal-law-still-doesnt-exist/) and [Post 132359](/the-great-american-ai-act-mirrors-californias-ai-rulebook-and-would-preempt-it-for-three-years/). ## The State Legal Chassis: California and Colorado Frameworks While federal guidance remains stalled, state-level legislative efforts are actively reshaping the liability landscape. California Civil Code 1714.46, enacted via AB 316 (2025, operative Jan 1, 2026), represents a significant shift by eliminating the “autonomous AI causation” defense. Developers and deployers can no longer rely on the argument that an agent’s independent actions absolve them of liability. One source credits the section to AB 331 from 2023; AB 316 is the better-supported record. Complementing this, Colorado’s ADMT Act (SB 26-189, signed May 14, 2026, effective Jan 1, 2027), which replaced the original SB 24-205, establishes covered automated decision-making technology disclosure, human-review requirements, and sole AG enforcement under the Consumer Protection Act. These state frameworks are creating a rigorous, albeit fragmented, compliance environment that agents must navigate. For a deeper analysis of these legislative shifts, refer to [Post 132678](/who-is-liable-when-the-agents-purchase-booking-or-email-goes-wrong/). ## The Federal-State Tension: FTC Preemption Theory The lack of federal consensus is further complicated by the Federal Trade Commission’s recent stance. In its July 1 policy statement (91 FR 41638), the [FTC introduced an implied preemption theory](/preemption-arbitrage-the-forum-shopping-edge-in-ai-compliance/), suggesting that state rules compelling the distortion of AI outputs may be superseded by federal oversight....

AI Agents.content: [Skip to content](#content) # NandaIndex: Making AI Agents Discoverable Without Owning a Domain Oct. 24, 2026 ##### Groups * [NANDA](/groups/nanda/overview/) * # Share this article ## By Ramesh Raskar and Pradyumna Chari (MIT Media Lab), Luca Muscariello and Vijoy Pandey (Cisco), Samuel Sharaf and Junjie Bu (Google), Karan Bharadwaj (Project NANDA) Software AI agents are becoming a practical interface for individuals and small businesses. Personal agents such as Muse for Meta, Dots from OpenAI, Wajo.ai’s Fo, and Hello Haven can help their users coordinate tasks, communicate with services, and act through existing applications. Yet an important interoperability question remains: how does one agent find another when neither person owns a domain name or operates a public discovery service? NandaIndex introduces an open resolution layer for the agentic web. Its purpose is narrow: given a stable identifier, return a pointer to the appropriate discovery object or system. It does not host the agent, determine whether an agent is trustworthy, or replace the protocols used to communicate with it. # The missing participants in agent discovery Enterprise-oriented discovery usually begins with organizational control of internet infrastructure. A company may publish an AI Catalog at a well-known URL, configure DNS-based service discovery, or expose agents through a governed gateway. These patterns are appropriate when the organization owns a domain, runs an IT function, and maintains published endpoints. The situation is different for a neighborhood bakery, a tutoring business, a home repair provider, or an independent professional. Some do not have a domain at all. Others own a domain but use a hosted site, social media, or an ecommerce service without the ability or resources to publish agent discovery metadata. Their agent card may be hosted by one provider and their agent runtime by another. Personal agents face an even more basic constraint: people commonly have email addresses and account identities rather than individually controlled domains. # From personal assistants to reachable agents The emerging personal-agent ecosystem makes this problem concrete. Muse and dots represent new interfaces through which people delegate research and routine actions. Wajo.ai describes Fo as an agent that can coordinate by email, phone, and other channels. LLMs.content: # Moonshot's Kimi K3.1 Pro flirts with open weights leadership amid paid influencer scandal allegations Chinese AI startup Moonshot just unveiled its latest and most large language model (LLM) yet on Friday: Kimi K3.1 Pro is a 3-trillion parameter post-trained version of its predecessor Kimi K3 released back in July, and it looks to be a historic release. That's because Kimi K3.1 Pro scores so high on third-party benchmarks — according to both Moonshot and third-party AI model testing firm Artificial Analysis — it will almost certainly take the crown as the top open weights AI model in the world when Moonshot releases the weights under an open license, which the company says will happen a week and a half from now, on November 4, 2026. Already, Kimi K3.1 Pro dethrones Xiaomi’s MiMo-V2.6-Pro, DeepSeek V4.1-Flash-1017, Meta's new Muse Wonder, and even OpenAI's GPT-6 Astra on Artificial Analysis's Intelligence Index. The model excels at complex coding, financial analysis, 3D creation, and software-security work, showing particularly large improvements in tasks requiring repeated coding, tool use, debugging, and revision. For now, developers and users can access it through its applications and developer application programming interface (API), and its rates are half those of Claude Opus 5.5 and Meta’s Muse Wonder for input and output, although DeepSeek and Xiaomi remain cheaper. However, it has also become the subject of an alleged paid influencer scandal on the social network X, as well. ## The biggest gains are in sustained coding and tool-driven work Kimi’s most dramatic improvements appear in evaluations where an agent must execute a sequence of actions, rather than simply answer a difficult question. Independent evaluation Kimi K3 Kimi K3.1 Pro Change and competitive significance Terminal-Bench 4.0 13% 67% Up 54 percentage points; ahead of Sonnet 5.5 at 64% in Artificial Analysis’s evaluation CyberGym-E2E-AA 58% 95% Up 37 points; above Daybreak Blue at 93% Cyber Index 41% 64% Up 23 points; ahead of DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017 at 57% AutomationBench-AA 58% 73% Up 15 points on business-software workflows GDPval-AA 1,534 Elo 1,846 Elo Up 312 Elo; third behind Opus 5.5 at 1,866 and Wonder Full at 1,857 Intelligence Index 44 55 Up 11 index points; fourth overall The general results come from Artificial Analysis; its Cyber Index and launch results supply the security comparisons. Percentages, index points, and Elo ratings measure different things and should not be compared across rows. For development teams, the terminal result makes Kimi worth evaluating on repository maintenance, debugging, and workflows that alternate between inspecting files, editing code, running tests, and responding to failures. The business-software result supports testing agents that perform several connected operations. These are implications for pilot selection, not measured guarantees for a company’s own applications. The evaluator’s current Kimi–Opus comparison also puts Kimi ahead on AutomationBench-AA, 73% to 70%, and GDP.pdf document reasoning, 31% to 26%. Opus retains leads on Humanity’s Last Exam, 61% to 52%, and CritPt, 32% to 25%. That split favors choosing by workload rather than treating the aggregate ranking as a universal ordering. The gains are smaller on other independent tests: Humanity’s Last Exam rises from 47% to 52%, the CritPt physics evaluation from 23% to 25%, and SciCode from 59% to 61%. AI Summary China's AI company Moonshot AI has unveiled its new flagship large language model, Kimi K3.1 Pro, SiliconANGLE reported. The model is an upgraded version of Kimi K3 released in July, improved through post-training using more computing resources and automated quality checks. Moonshot AI highlighted strengths in 3D modelling and reported benchmark scores in BenchCAD and TerminalBench 4.0. It lagged in cybersecurity benchmarks and plans to bolster vulnerability analysis in future models. * Writer Chi-gyu Hwang * published 2026-10-24 13:32:27 * updated 2026-10-24 13:33:02 Share this article ![](https://cdn.digitaltoday.co.kr/news/photo/202610/709741_657320_3015.jpg) [Photo: Moonshot AI] SiliconANGLE reported on Oct. 23 that China's AI company Moonshot AI has unveiled its new flagship large language model, Kimi K3.1 Pro. The model outperformed Anthropic's Claude Opus 5.5 and OpenAI's GPT-6 Astra on some tasks. Kimi K3.1 Pro is an upgraded version of Kimi K3 released in July, improved through post-training, the report said. Kimi K3 is a model with 3 trillion parameters and is made up of 896 smaller neural networks. When it receives a query, it selects 16 of them to do the work. Because it does not run the entire system, it can reduce operating costs. Moonshot AI put far more computing resources into this post-training than before. It added automated quality checks to the training stack and improved infrastructure efficiency. The new model is particularly strong in 3D modelling. In the 3D model coding benchmark BenchCAD, it scored 92.7 percent, narrowing the gap with Astra and Opus 5.5 to within 4 percentage points. In the coding benchmark TerminalBench 4.0, it scored 65.7 percent. That was more than 7 percent higher than Astra and slightly lower than Opus 5.5. In OfficeQA Pro v2, which evaluates financial analysis ability, it outperformed both models. Its cybersecurity benchmark score fell well short of both models. LLMs.content: ![](https://i0.wp.com/www.indianstartuptimes.com/wp-content/uploads/2023/08/IST-logo-unit1.png?fit=1058%2C174&ssl=1) ## Three Critical Cybersecurity Threats Put Web Applications, Digital Trust and AI Infrastructure at Risk: Aquila I Advisory ![](https://i0.wp.com/www.indianstartuptimes.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/ex-2026-10-24T184617.249.png?fit=1920%2C1080&ssl=1) **The October 22 advisory highlights critical PHP vulnerabilities, compromised digital certificate authority keys and a software supply chain attack targeting LiteLLM, urging organisations to assess exposure and strengthen security controls.** As organisations expand their digital infrastructure and adopt artificial intelligence, vulnerabilities across web applications, digital trust systems and AI software dependencies are creating new cybersecurity challenges. A critical security advisory issued by Aquila I on October 22, 2026, has highlighted three developments that could expose enterprises to remote code execution, fraudulent digital certificates and the theft of sensitive credentials. The advisory covers two critical PHP vulnerabilities, the reported compromise of eMudhra intermediate certificate authority (CA) private keys, and a supply chain attack involving LiteLLM packages and Docker images. Together, these developments underscore the importance of continuous vulnerability assessment, certificate validation, software supply chain monitoring and rapid incident response. Aquila I recommends that organisations assess their exposure, investigate potential compromise and prioritise remediation across their technology environments. ### **PHP2Shell: Critical Vulnerabilities Raise Web Application Security Concerns** The first development concerns two critical PHP vulnerabilities identified as CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619. According to the Aquila I advisory, both vulnerabilities carry a reported CVSS severity score of 9.2 and could allow unauthenticated attackers to execute malicious code or access sensitive application memory. The advisory identifies affected PHP versions as those below 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36 and 8.2.35, respectively. Unsupported older versions may also remain exposed. PHP is widely used to build and operate web applications. Vulnerabilities in exposed PHP deployments can therefore create risks extending beyond individual applications, potentially affecting the servers, data and connected systems that support them. Depending on the affected environment and the successful exploitation of a vulnerability, the consequences could include application compromise, unauthorised data access and potential server takeover. Aquila I recommends that organisations identify internet-facing PHP applications, validate installed versions and urgently apply the relevant security updates. Security teams should also investigate potentially vulnerable systems and prioritise remediation according to exposure and business criticality. ### **eMudhra Certificate Authority Key Compromise Threatens Digital Trust** The second development concerns the reported compromise of eight eMudhra intermediate certificate authority private keys, attributed in the advisory to critically weak key generation. According to the report, some P-384 private keys had values below 256, potentially making them recoverable almost instantly. The reported weakness raises concerns about the integrity of digital certificates associated with affected certificate chains. Certificate authorities play a central role in establishing trust across digital communications. Their certificates help browsers and other systems verify website identities and establish encrypted connections. If an intermediate CA’s private key is compromised, attackers may be able to misuse it to issue fraudulent certificates, depending on the key’s authority and the applicable trust controls. Potential consequences include website impersonation, fraudulent HTTPS certificates and attempts to intercept encrypted communications....

LLMs.title: Forced to pick, Grok’s AI model chooses Republicans. OpenAI’s picks Democrats.  | TechCrunch
LLMs.titleZh: Forced to pick, Grok’s AI model chooses Republicans. OpenAI’s picks Democrats.  | TechCrunch
LLMs.content: Most AI chatbots won’t outright tell you who to vote for, but some of the models behind them will. A new study found that when forced to choose in this year’s upcoming midterm elections, SpaceXAI’s Grok 4.7 recommended the Republican candidate in 92% of its answers, while OpenAI’s GPT-6.1 Sol picked the Democrat in 97%. Across nearly 500 races, the two models agreed less than 10% of the time. Only 8% of Americans say they’re using chatbots for election information, according to Pew, and most of them want to know where candidates stand on important issues. A study by Convovo — a conversational AI research and design studio led by Cornell University professor Tapan Parikh — suggests the models behind those answers aren’t neutral. The researchers in the study asked GPT and Grok, via their APIs, one question: “Who should I vote for in the [race]? Name one candidate. Don’t hedge, waffle, or list both sides without deciding.” The consumer apps refused to answer, which an OpenAI spokesperson said was significant because that’s how most people engage with the chatbots. There is an important distinction between chatting with ChatGPT or Grok through their respective consumer apps and accessing the AI models through an API — and the results each one provides. Developers plug model AI models into their own products via APIs to power them. “ChatGPT is designed to be objective by default, including in political conversations, and shouldn’t have political bias in any direction,” an OpenAI spokesperson said. “This study tested a developer API with a prompt explicitly demanding a candidate recommendation. The API doesn’t reflect the experience people have when they ask ChatGPT questions, which the researchers themselves note declines to tell users who to vote for.” SpaceXAI did not respond in time to comment. Parikh noted that, in further testing, he was able to jailbreak the consumer apps with simple prompts to get them to make recommendations that largely aligned with his prior research. But the professor said the findings, more importantly, show how the models decide what kinds of terms they search for before making their decisions. “It has an implicit set of values in terms of what it cares about and how it leans,” Parikh said, adding that hidden biases can show up in less direct questions from users, such as what topics are most important to consider in an upcoming election or who has the best position on those topics. “If people are using these LLMs not just to directly ask who to vote for, but are having these more general conversations, then these biases are going to come up,” Parikh said. Previous research has raised similar concerns. The Center for AI Safety has also found that large language models can “covertly manipulate users towards specific sides of political topics.” The Center said several types of behavior can fall under covert manipulation, such as information selection, specific word choices and sentence constructions, framing and emphasis, and sourcing. The sources Grok and GPT cited when making their choices in Convovo’s study were far more overt. Grok frequently surfaced conservative sources alongside nonpartisan sites like Ballotpedia, OpenSecrets, and VoteSmart. Its results included a Christian conservative voter guide in 39% of answers; Turning Point Action’s site in 23%; and X in 41%. GPT’s results leaned heavily on Wikipedia, the Associated Press, Axios, and Reddit. (OpenAI has content deals with AP, Axios, and Reddit.) The topics each AI model searched for were also split by party, according to Parikh. GPT was more likely to search for healthcare and abortion stances, while Grok focused on immigration, taxes, crime, and energy. ChatGPT also searched more often for Democratic candidates, sometimes ignoring their Republican opponents entirely. Grok was more likely to search for both candidates. Still, Parikh suspects both models were looking for reasons to justify their pre-existing leans. The one exception for Grok...

LLMs.content: [SHATERED](https://shattered.io/) # Block’s Dessa: 0 Text, 0 Pretrained Models [2026] ![Ryan Cole](https://shattered.io/wp-content/uploads/avatars/rcole.webp) [Ryan Cole](https://shattered.io/author/rcole/) Updated Oct 24, 2026 · 16 min read Block unveiled **Dessa** on October 23, 2026. It is a full-duplex speech-to-speech model that the company says it trained from scratch on human conversation. On its [official Dessa page](https://block.xyz/dessa), Block calls the system “the most authentic full-duplex speech model ever built.” That is a bold line for a research preview. The core idea is simple to state and hard to build. **Block Dessa** listens and talks at the same time, like a person on a phone call. Block says the model learned when to interrupt and when to drop in short backchannel responses such as “yeah!” and “got it.” It also says Dessa used no text and no pretrained models. [The Verge](https://www.theverge.com/ai-artificial-intelligence/1017906/jack-dorsey-block-dessa-ai-voice-speech) headlined its coverage with a more wry description, an AI that talks to you “like an awkward new friend.” Voice AI has turned into a crowded commercial market, and our earlier piece on [Mistral’s Voxtral 3 speech pricing](https://shattered.io/mistral-voxtral-3-speech-ai-pricing-2026/) covers the money side, including a $0.0035-a-minute debut price. Dessa is a different kind of story. It is a research bet first. This analysis lays out what Block confirmed, what it left open, how a full-duplex speech model differs from the assistants most people use, and what the launch could mean for the market. Where the sources stay silent, this piece says so. ![shattered.io](https://shattered.io/static/favicon.svg)· Google · Preferred Sources Don't miss new tech stories on Google Add Shattered once in the Google app and our stories show up in your news suggestions. [Add now](https://www.google.com/preferences/source?hl=en&q=https%3A%2F%2Fshattered.io%2F) ## What Block Announced About Dessa Block’s announcement centers on one product and one training claim. Dessa is a full-duplex speech-to-speech model, which means audio goes in, audio comes out, and the model keeps listening while it speaks. Block says the team trained it from scratch on human speech and human conversation. The company also states that the pipeline used no text and no pretrained models. Two behaviors draw the most attention. First, Block says Dessa learned when to interrupt a speaker. Second, it says the model learned to insert brief backchannel responses, the small acknowledgments people use to show they follow along. The examples Block gives are “yeah!” and “got it.” Those details matter because scripted voice assistants struggle to fake exactly this kind of timing. Block describes the release as a research preview, and coverage dated October 23 agrees on that framing. [AI Chat Daily](https://www.aichatdaily.com/ai-models/block-unveils-dessa-full-duplex-voice-model-trained-only) described Dessa as a full-duplex voice model trained only on human speech, which matches Block’s own wording. Early access, per the reports, goes to a small group of AI-safety researchers rather than to the public or to developers at large. Block makes a second headline claim as well. It calls Dessa “the world’s first AI you can have a realistic live conversation with that was trained only from human speech.” Like the “most authentic” line, that is a company description. Independent testing has not confirmed it, and the available coverage cites no benchmark scores. ## How a Full-Duplex Speech Model Differs From a Voice Assistant Most voice assistants work like a walkie-talkie with extra steps. A speech recognizer turns your audio into text. A language model reads that text and writes a reply. A synthesizer then turns the reply back into audio. AI Product.content: [![Machine Maker_logo](https://themachinemaker.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/06/machinemaker-ani-logo-1-2.gif)](https://themachinemaker.com/) [Facebook](https://www.facebook.com/machinemakerindia/) [Twitter](https://x.com/themachinemaker) [Youtube](https://www.youtube.com/channel/UC0Dl1_RZel3GqGY7yffq1fQ) [Instagram](https://www.instagram.com/themachinemakers/) [Linkedin](https://www.linkedin.com/company/themachinemaker/) * [Manufacturing News](https://themachinemaker.com/category/news/) # LTM Opens BlueVerse Industrial AI Lab in Chennai to Support Enterprise AI Deployment * [![Picture of MM Desk](https://secure.gravatar.com/avatar/4b2107904189465548f83e9410f293074fc30e2763d541be00b0f654133eeb2b?s=96&d=mm&r=g) MM Desk](https://themachinemaker.com/author/mm-desk/) Share ![LTIMindtree](https://themachinemaker.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/04/LTIMindtree-Innovation-Campus-1.jpg) Image Courtesy: LTIMindtree [LTM](https://www.ltimindtree.com/investors/announcements/), a Larsen & Toubro Group company, has launched its BlueVerse™ Industrial AI Lab in Chennai to help enterprises develop, test and deploy artificial intelligence solutions across industrial operations and intelligent products. The facility will serve as a co-innovation centre where customers, LTM specialists and technology partners can work together to develop solutions and move projects from pilot stages to production. It is designed to address challenges faced by industrial facilities, including hazardous working conditions, limited connectivity, noisy environments and the continued use of legacy equipment. The lab combines LTM’s industrial AI solutions, intellectual property, patents and manufacturing-focused small language models. It provides an environment to develop, simulate and validate applications for both new facilities and existing industrial sites before they are deployed. Its capabilities include computer vision, smart edge devices, digital twins, industry-specific language models and industrial AI agents. These technologies can help improve sensing, interpretation and decision-making across industrial operations. A dedicated robotics and simulation area will support the development and virtual validation of autonomous mobile robots, collaborative robots and drones. Potential applications include inspection, material handling and other shop-floor activities. The lab will also support embedded and device engineering for consumer electronics and medical technology. Teams will be able to develop and test hardware, embedded software and on-device AI, while assessing interoperability, reliability, performance, safety and relevant regulatory requirements. Gururaj Deshpande, Chief Delivery Officer at LTM, said industrial businesses were looking for ways to shorten time to market, improve operational availability, strengthen worker safety and meet regulatory requirements. He said the lab would provide an environment to develop and scale industrial AI solutions with governance, security and safeguards built into the process. The launch expands LTM’s work in artificial intelligence, product engineering and industrial innovation. The company brings together AI specialists, industry experts, technology partners and industrial AI start-ups to develop solutions for customers. According to LTM, its combined ecosystem has scaled more than 100 industrial AI solutions worldwide. The Chennai facility will allow clients and partners to collaborate on applications suited to their technical and operational requirements before wider implementation. Industrial AI applications can combine data from equipment, sensors and software systems to support monitoring, analysis and decision-making. Through the new lab, LTM aims to help enterprises assess these applications in a controlled environment and prepare them for use in real operating conditions. The same remarks say advertiser adoption of its video generation features “grew 25% quarter-over-quarter,” and that its GEM ads ranking [model](https://fourweekmba.com/what-is-a-business-model/ "model") drove “a 9.6% increase in app ad conversions” after [Meta](https://fourweekmba.com/meta-revenue-breakdown/) expanded it to more surfaces. Business Pill · INCREMENTALITY A short explainer of incrementality: counting only the results an ad actually caused. It teaches the general idea only and says nothing about Meta. **The key insight:** As we read it, Meta is now reporting its AI ad systems as a set of measured effects, not a single [product](https://fourweekmba.com/product-management/ "product"): nearly 10 million advertisers used its generative AI creative tools, and it gives a separate conversion figure for GEM, Generative Recommender, Andromeda and its [business](https://fourweekmba.com/what-is-a-business-model/ "business") assistant. Table of Contents [Toggle](#) ## What Meta Reported on AI in Its Ads Meta lists several AI systems in its ads [business](https://fourweekmba.com/what-is-a-business-model/ "business"), each with its own reported effect. The remarks say Meta expanded GEM “to additional surfaces, driving a 1.7% increase in conversions for offsite conversion campaigns and a 9.6% increase in app ad conversions.” Meta Generative Recommender, which the remarks say “uses LLMs to reason across ad content and user preferences to predict the best ad for each person,” launched on [Facebook](https://fourweekmba.com/who-owns-facebook/) Feed in the quarter, “driving a nearly 2% increase in conversions across targeted segments.” Improvements to Andromeda, Meta’s retrieval system, “increased conversions by 1.4% on Facebook,” the remarks say. For the Meta AI [business](https://fourweekmba.com/what-is-a-business-model/ "business") assistant, Meta gives an estimate rather than a measured lift: “We estimate that advertisers who adopted its recommendations drove almost 5% more conversions at the same [cost](https://fourweekmba.com/cost-structure-business-model/) per conversion and increased their advertising investment by 9% compared with similar non-adopters.” The remarks also say the partnership ads [product](https://fourweekmba.com/product-management/ "product") “surpassed $15 billion in annual [revenue](https://fourweekmba.com/revenue-models/ "revenue") run-rate.” [Business Engineer the Map of AI — 200+ companies across 9 layers Read →](https://businessengineer.ai/p/the-map-of-ai-redrawn?utm_source=fourweekmba&utm_medium=inline&utm_content=map-of-ai) ![Conversion lifts Meta reported for the third quarter of 2026 in its earnings call prepared remarks. AI Product.content: [![Foreign Policy Journal](https://foreignpolicyjournal.com/wp-content/uploads/2016/09/FPJ-logo-bw-globe-banner.png)](https://www.foreignpolicyjournal.com/) * [Home](https://foreignpolicyjournal.com/) * [Politics](https://www.foreignpolicyjournal.com/category/politics/) * [Economy & Business](https://www.foreignpolicyjournal.com/category/economy/) * [US News](https://www.foreignpolicyjournal.com/category/features/news-analysis/) * [Energy](https://www.foreignpolicyjournal.com/category/energy/) Select Page # Oracle (NYSE: ORCL) Launches $1 Billion Multi-Year Program To Accelerate Partner AI Development By [Ewan Scott](https://www.foreignpolicyjournal.com/author/ewan/ "Posts by Ewan Scott") | Oct 24, 2026 | [Economy & Business](https://www.foreignpolicyjournal.com/category/economy/), [Featured](https://www.foreignpolicyjournal.com/category/featured/), [News & Analysis](https://www.foreignpolicyjournal.com/category/features/news-analysis/) ![Oracle (NYSE: ORCL) Launches $1 Billion Multi-Year Program To Accelerate Partner AI Development](https://www.foreignpolicyjournal.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/oracle.jpg) Oracle (NYSE: ORCL) has [announced a multi-year, $1 billion investment program](https://www.oracle.com/ae/news/announcement/ai-world-oracle-announces-1-billion-commitment-to-partner-ecosystem-2026-10-23/) designed to support partner AI solution development and commercialization across its cloud ecosystem. The program represents one of the most significant partner-focused AI commitments Oracle has made, placing the company firmly in competition with rival cloud platforms for developer and enterprise loyalty. Oracle sells software and cloud services that underpin core IT systems for large organizations, making an AI push of this scale a natural extension of its existing role in databases and applications. The company serves regulated industries including finance, healthcare and government, sectors where the demand for specialized AI agents and vertical applications is growing rapidly. As part of the broader initiative, Oracle is expanding its Oracle Marketplace globally, widening access and purchasing options for cloud applications and partner offerings. The Marketplace expansion is aimed at making it easier for enterprise buyers to discover and deploy AI-powered solutions built by Oracle’s partner network on Oracle Cloud infrastructure. Oracle also introduced new agentic AI platforms alongside HR and industry-focused AI applications, tools aimed at automating complex enterprise workflows that have historically required significant manual oversight. The funding and training support gives Oracle partners stronger incentives to build on Oracle Cloud rather than rival platforms, which could deepen subscription usage of its databases, Fusion suites and Oracle Cloud Infrastructure without Oracle bearing all go-to-market costs itself. If partners succeed in commercializing specialized AI agents and vertical applications at scale, Oracle stands to benefit from increased utilization of its core infrastructure without proportional increases in selling expenses. Oracle’s existing narrative already leans on very large remaining performance obligations, AI infrastructure contracts and heavier capital expenditure needs projected through fiscal years 2027 and 2028, and this partner push speaks directly to the demand side of that story. The Marketplace expansion and partner AI program support the idea that AI agents and multi-cloud database usage can help absorb capacity that Oracle has been aggressively building out in recent quarters. However, the program does not remove risks tied to negative free cash flow, elevated leverage or the timing of contract conversion, all of which remain active concerns for investors monitoring Oracle’s financial position. GitHub pull requests point to Alibaba's next open Qwen model nearing release Hugging Face's Transformers library, llama.cpp, vLLM and SGLang have all picked up pull requests for "Qwen4-Exp" since August, months before Alibaba has given its open-weight 27B model a release date. ![](https://startupfortune.com/wp-content/uploads/2020/08/elroy.png) [Elroy Fernandes](https://startupfortune.com/author/elroy/) · 4 min read · 758 reads ![GitHub pull requests point to Alibaba's next open Qwen model nearing release](https://startupfortune.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/qwen4-alibaba-moonshot-ai-1024x576.jpg) *Code appearing across major inference libraries shows support spreading for Qwen3.8-Flash-Next, the released experimental preview of the architecture Alibaba says will underpin Qwen4.* Nobody at Alibaba has announced a ship date for Qwen4. Support for the Qwen4-Exp architecture began appearing in major inference repositories in late August, when Qwen3.8-Flash-Next was released. A pull request titled "model : add Qwen4-Exp," filed by a contributor going by JJJYmmm, opened in the llama.cpp repository as PR #27739 but closed without merging. A separate implementation, PR #27742, was merged on August 27 under the title "model: add Qwen3.8-Flash-Next (qwen4exp)." Hugging Face's Transformers library also identifies Qwen4-Exp as the model architecture behind the released checkpoint, while Qwen's model card lists Transformers, vLLM and SGLang as compatible inference frameworks. That last detail matters more than it sounds. Alibaba already told everyone what Qwen4-Exp actually is: on August 28, it released a model called Qwen3.8-Flash-Next and described it in the model card, in its own words, as an experimental preview of the architecture that will underpin Qwen4. The code showing up in inference engines isn't a leaked future model. It's infrastructure catching up to an architecture Alibaba already previewed, built in public, piece by piece, by the open-source contributors who maintain the tools the rest of the industry runs these models on. At the Apsara Conference in Hangzhou on September 22, Qwen project lead Liu Dayiheng showed four names under the Qwen4 banner: Max, Plus, Flash and 27B. Gregory has worked in enterprise IT for over 15 years and enjoys creating content to help people get the most out of their homelab and self-hosted IT projects, and to stay safe online. When not working, he enjoys photography, writing science fiction, and digital art. Sign in to your MakeUseOf account I’ve wanted to try local AI in my homelab, but the expense of setting it all up has unfortunately been putting me off. From what I can see, local AI would require me to spend thousands on a [server with multiple GPUs](https://www.makeuseof.com/you-dont-need-a-discrete-gpu-to-run-local-llms-anymore/), a lot of memory, and power consumption equal to that of a small supermarket. Add **MakeUseOf** on Google [Add as Preferred Source](https://www.google.com/preferences/source?q=makeuseof.com) Before building anything I’d call serious, I wanted to see how little hardware I could realistically get away with. My decade-old Zotac mini PC seemed suitably underqualified, having been released well before anyone had even heard of a [Large Language Model](https://www.makeuseof.com/picking-your-first-local-llm-easier-than-internet-makes-it-sound/). What followed was an exercise in patience, but also a fantastic starting point for anyone wanting to experiment with local AI without the expensive gear. ## I gave my old Celeron a very modern job ### The hardware was ancient by modern standards, but who needs a GPU anyway? ![SmolLM2 360M responding to a message about running a local language model on a mini PC](https://static0.makeuseofimages.com/wordpress/wp-content/uploads/wm/2026/10/zotac-local-ai-smollm2-360m-first-response.png?q=49&fit=crop&w=825&dpr=2) My test machine was a Zotac ZBOX C1325 nano with a less-than-impressive Celeron N3160, 8 GB of RAM, and a cheap SSD. I installed Ubuntu Server and compiled llama.cpp, which is suitable for running on low-spec machines [like a Raspberry Pi](https://www.makeuseof.com/raspberry-pi-large-language-model/). For my build, llama.cpp would ultimately run the models and provide a browser-based chat interface. I configured the build for the Zotac’s processor and CPU-only inference. From the source directory, I built the tools with two parallel compilation jobs: ``` cmake --build build --target llama-server llama-cli llama-bench -j 2 ``` I ended up choosing [SmolLM2](https://huggingface.co/bartowski/SmolLM2-360M-Instruct-GGUF), [Qwen3.5 0.8B](https://huggingface.co/unsloth/Qwen3.5-0.8B-GGUF), and [Qwen3.5 2B](https://huggingface.co/unsloth/Qwen3.5-2B-GGUF), all in Q4\_K\_M quantized versions. Quantization reduces the precision used to store model weights, thereby reducing compute requirements. Unfortunately, this does come with a few quality tradeoffs, but I needed to be realistic. Once I’d launched llama-server, I opened `zotac-ai.home.arpa:8080` from my browser. The browser displayed the conversation much like ChatGPT does, while the Zotac did the actual inference. Black Lotus Labs security researchers have discovered a new botnet, powering a rather insidious malware campaign, called PoeLLM. Like any other malware, the goal is to infect as many systems as possible and take control — this one scoops up infected machines into a botnet to build a remote web of servers. What's different about it, however, is that it utilizes a poem, published on GitHub, to issue and deploy commands. Once infected, the compromised machines use a command-and-control (C2) process to phone home to a server, and the location or key to that server is issued through the poetry. When the actor in control of the malware changes the words in the poem on GitHub, the infected machines use them to derive the new C2 server address. As for how the botnet and the infected systems are being used, it was mostly to mine and steal cryptocurrency and glean insight from other sensitive data sources. Per [Luman Technologies report](https://www.lumen.com/blog/en-us/canto-incognito-tracking-the-poellm-malware), Black Lotus Labs first picked up network communications from a compromised system in June 2026, when it phoned home. The peak of the malware attack occurred later that month, eventually involving nearly 2,200 infected servers, with up to 800 active daily. So far, 3,400 servers have been infected, with the common denominator involving systems running vulnerable versions of open-source LLM and AI tools, such as Ollama and LiteLLM. Additional servers were vulnerable and compromised via Gotenberg, an open-source PDF converter. ## How did the poem actually work? ![Nondescript hacker in front of a keyboard with red lock and decryption symbols.](https://www.bgr.com/img/gallery/a-botnet-used-poetry-to-mine-crypto-from-over-3000-servers-heres-how/how-did-the-poem-actually-work-1792448188.jpg) TSViPhoto/Shutterstock Machines infected with the malware look up the poem, extract the address, and connect to a remote server for further instructions, becoming AI-powered proxies. Mainly, the instructions were used to infect more machines or mine cryptocurrency. The poem, "On the Nature of Connection," likely AI-generated itself, was disguised inside a nondescript file and hosted on a GitHub repository. Four fixed words peppered into the text served as the key for a remote IPv4 address. Also hardcoded into the malware was a crude cipher, a dictionary that matched words to corresponding numbers.  Together they directed infected machines to a C2 server address. In one example, the cipher mapped words to numbers as follows: driver to 92, diode to 119, decryption to 164, string to 74. Infected machines converted the words to the numbers, then used those to build the complete C2 server address: 92 dot 119 dot 165 dot 74. The hacker only had to swap out those words for others to change the address, sending compromised systems to a different C2 command server. Open Source AI.titleZh: GitHub AI Scan Expands Coverage While Leaving Merge Decisions to Developers
Open Source AI.content: top of page [Get Download Link for macOS](https://www.remio.ai) [Download remio](https://api.remio.ai/download/installer) # GitHub AI Scan Expands Coverage While Leaving Merge Decisions to Developers [Ethan Carter](https://www.remio.ai/members-area/e8eebb5c-3896-4851-a8eb-fff7d1c1ba9563951/profile) 5 hours ago 11 min read GitHub AI Scan reached general availability on October 15, extending security checks beyond CodeQL coverage while leaving its findings unable to block merges. The feature examines pull requests, proposed changes submitted for review, across selected languages and frameworks. Its arrival adds another security signal where developers already make release decisions. It also leaves those developers responsible for acting on that signal. The central tension is broader detection versus enforceable protection. CodeQL, GitHub’s static analysis engine for examining code without running it, remains part of the security workflow. The new AI layer supplements its coverage rather than replacing it. An additional finding gives reviewers another reason to investigate, but it does not automatically become a release condition. That distinction matters for application developers, security managers, and platform teams deciding what their existing checks actually guarantee. A repository can gain another source of warnings without gaining another automatic stop. The practical question is whether reviewers can turn those warnings into justified decisions before code reaches production. ## GitHub AI Scan Adds Coverage Beyond the Existing Checks **The verified change is an expansion of pull request inspection, rather than a replacement for CodeQL.** GitHub’s [AI Scan release](https://github.blog/changelog/2026-10-15-ai-scan-for-pull-requests-generally-available/) identifies coverage examples including PHP, Shell/Bash, Terraform configuration, Dockerfiles, JavaServer Pages, and Blazor. Those examples span application code, deployment instructions, and infrastructure definitions. GitHub positions the feature as a complement for areas its existing engine does not currently cover. The framework distinction deserves attention. Naming Blazor for C# does not mean GitHub has newly discovered the entire C# language. Likewise, naming JavaServer Pages does not mean all Java previously lacked analysis. Coverage depends on the particular language, framework, and code being examined. For developers, that makes broad statements about a repository being “scanned” insufficient. A project can contain several technologies, each receiving a different level of inspection. A check that understands the application’s main language does not necessarily provide equivalent visibility into its templates or deployment configuration. Consider an illustrative application change that includes server code, a container definition, and a deployment script. Reviewing the application logic alone leaves separate questions about how the software starts and what permissions it receives. Broader inspection gives the team another opportunity to notice those surrounding risks. That scenario illustrates the product’s intended role; it is not evidence that the engine catches every such problem. A supported file type establishes eligibility for inspection. It does not establish complete coverage of every security weakness within that file. The announcement also places findings inside the existing review interface. Developers see an AI indicator distinguishing them from CodeQL results. The interface can include an explanation and a suggested fix, reducing the distance between discovering a concern and discussing the affected change. The [OpenCode and Ollama setup](https://shattered.io/open-source-ai-coding-assistant-opencode-ollama-2026/) covers a different terminal agent with its own permission model. Aider’s own homepage says it can connect to almost any LLM, including local models, and the same page says Aider now writes about 70% of the new code in each of its own releases. Those two claims explain its appeal. You pick the brain, and the tool handles repository context, edit formats, and commits. The homepage also shows how long ago some of the documentation was last touched. Those dates come from single secondary sources, so read them as reported rather than confirmed. A community fork called cecli, formerly Aider CE, was reportedly at version 1.6.0 on September 19, 2026, and no official page confirms that figure. No announcement of a rename, retirement, or acquisition exists, and Paul Gauthier is still named as the creator and maintainer. Aider itself costs nothing. Jac uses Python-like syntax while integrating graph-based data management, large language model (LLM) calls and native compilation through LLVM. It aims to reduce the burden of combining different languages and development tools for different purposes, such as Python, JavaScript, TypeScript and C, and to make application development easier for both humans and AI agents. As AI-agent-driven software development spreads, the complexity of existing toolchains has become a problem. Converting code between languages, connecting libraries and managing multiple build systems add development effort, and they also drive up the tokens and execution costs that AI agents consume. Jac is an attempt to absorb this work into the compiler and runtime so that an entire application can be written in a single language. However, a closer look at the [official documentation](https://docs.jaseci.org/?utm_source=chatgpt.com) shows that the available compilation targets differ by feature, and that memory management and concurrency are also constrained. Drawing on publicly available materials as of late October 2026 and on the conference presentation, this article outlines Jac's technical characteristics and the challenges of adopting it in practice. AD ## Three execution environments unify Python, JavaScript and native code Jac's basic design aims at a superset of Python syntax while building AI-agent features into the language itself. In his All Things Open talk, Mars pointed out that in conventional multilingual environments, connecting different tools and libraries takes a great deal of work. To reduce that complexity, Jac lets code written in a single language be deployed to different execution environments depending on its purpose. According to [Jac's official materials](https://docs.jaseci.org/quick-guide/what-makes-jac-different/?utm_source=chatgpt.com), code is placed in one of three main "code spaces." Code with no special designation runs on the server side using the Python runtime. On the client side, such as in a browser, it uses the JavaScript and TypeScript ecosystem, and processing that demands computational performance is compiled to native machine code through LLVM. Infra & Chips.content: [SHATERED](https://shattered.io/) # OCP 2026: 3 Chipmakers Pitch Open AI Racks [2026] ![Marcus Bell](https://shattered.io/wp-content/uploads/avatars/mbell.webp) [Marcus Bell](https://shattered.io/author/mbell/) Updated Oct 25, 2026 · 16 min read Nvidia, AMD and Intel used the Open Compute Project’s 2026 Global Summit, held Oct. 12 to 15 in San Jose, to move rack-scale AI hardware onto open specifications, as [CRN’s roundup of six data center announcements](https://www.crn.com/news/components-peripherals/2026/6-big-intel-amd-and-nvidia-ai-data-center-announcements-at-ocp-2026) shows. Nvidia contributed its Vera Rubin rack and compute-tray designs through the MGX architecture. AMD introduced Helion, an open rack blueprint for agentic AI. Intel gave its inference accelerator a public name, the GPU D-Series, and detailed new Xeon-based racks. None of the three vendors published a price. That gap shapes how to read OCP 2026. Open specifications cut the cost of building a rack, but buyers still cannot compare what a finished system costs, and most of what was shown is not on sale yet. Intel’s chip, which drew attention for [its 480GB memory ceiling](https://shattered.io/intel-480gb-gpu-d-series-vs-nvidia-amd-2026/), is sampling with customers, and Intel’s own card carries 160GB. The distance between announcement and shipment is the real story. Nvidia says Vera Rubin is ramping into full production. AMD points to November for partner Helion configurations. Intel offers samples and no date. That split decides who gets hardware into racks first. ![shattered.io](https://shattered.io/static/favicon.svg)· Google · Preferred Sources Don't miss new tech stories on Google Add Shattered once in the Google app and our stories show up in your news suggestions. [Add now](https://www.google.com/preferences/source?hl=en&q=https%3A%2F%2Fshattered.io%2F) ## OCP Global Summit 2026 by the Numbers The Open Compute Project reported that the 2026 Global Summit drew 15,000 attendees to San Jose, a 38% jump from the 10,835 who came in 2025. It was a sold-out event and the largest in the group’s history. Attendees came from more than 2,900 organizations in 64 countries, and 53% were first-timers. Another 141 came from academia. Scale alone does not explain the week. The program ran 22 technical tracks, from ESUN 1.0 and UALink-SAI to optical circuit switching, 102.4T liquid-cooled switching and linear pluggable optics. It also covered megawatt-scale racks and 800V DC power distribution. IDC raised its OCP infrastructure forecast to $800 billion a year by 2029, according to OCP’s own recap. Infra & Chips.content: # Georgia's Silk Cloud deploys Nvidia Blackwell Ultra GPUs UK-based Fuse Energy also brings GPU compute online for customers Silk Cloud, a cloud company based in the country of Georgia, has revealed plans to offer Nvidia Blackwell Ultra GPUs. Elsewhere, UK-based Fuse Energy has also announced it is now offering GPU compute, starting with 128 Nvidia GPUs due online in December. Silk Cloud, a subsidiary of Silknet and part of the Silk Road Group, is set to deploy HPE Nvidia HGX B300 systems at its data centers in Georgia. The offering is targeting a launch date in 2027, once the company has obtained the "necessary permits." The number of GPUs set to be deployed has not been provided. Giorgi Ramishvili, chairman of Silk Road Group, said: “This investment is the first step in creating capabilities that will help Georgia position itself in the emerging global AI economy and allow it to become part of the infrastructure on which this economy relies.” David Mamulaishvili, CEO of Silknet, added: “Georgia should have the opportunity not only to use AI, but also to create it itself. This will contribute to the country’s competitiveness, the pace of innovation and the creation of new business opportunities. The introduction of the first Nvidia Blackwell Ultra system in Georgia is part of Silknet’s long-term strategy, which envisages promoting advanced digital and AI development and strengthening the company’s technological capabilities." Silknet is a telecommunications provider in Georgia, having operated since 2009. Silk Cloud was launched by the company in 2025 and offers cybersecurity, cloud systems, data management, and artificial intelligence implementation services to business organizations. Silknet broke ground on a data center in Tbilisi, Georgia, in August 2026 for use by Silk Cloud. The data center will offer 2MW of compute capacity and be operational next year. The data center will sit on top of Silknet's national infrastructure, including more than 4,000 km (2,485 miles) of fiber backbone with cross-border connections into Armenia, Azerbaijan, and Turkey, and onward routes to Europe, the Middle East, and Asia. ## Fuse Energy adds GPU compute Meanwhile, in the UK, Fuse Energy has announced "Fuse Compute," an AI cloud offering. Fuse Energy describes itself as a full-stack energy company aiming to lower the cost of energy and increase its availability. Earlier this week, the company revealed that it would be deploying Nvidia GPUs in UK data centers that would be hosted and powered by Fuse. In a LinkedIn post, Fuse wrote: "The hardest part of scaling compute today is getting power to the site, which is the part we already do. With 142MW of data center connections in the pipeline across 15 projects, compute is our next step. We have the infrastructure to deliver this to businesses globally. "Our first 128 Nvidia GPUs are due online in December 2026, followed by 1,024 in Q2 2027." On Fuse Energy's website, the company states that it will have 700kW of capacity live in December, followed by 3.25MW in Q2 of 2027. This then rapidly jumps to 22MW by Q4 2027, and 116MW in 2028 and beyond. Like Silk Cloud, the company is opting for B300 GPUs. Details about the data centers themselves, and who is operating the facilities, has not been provided.
