Infra & Chips.content: [![datacenters logo](/_icons/logos/datacenters-logo-header.svg?mod=2)](/) * [AI & Compute Infrastructure](/news/ai-compute-infrastructure) * 2 minRead # AI workloads reshape data centre power efficiency Artificial intelligence (AI) workloads are driving a re-evaluation of data centre power design, shifting focus from peak efficiency to flat-load performance. Traditional low-voltage architectures struggle with the dynamic and high-density demands of GPU clusters. * [ETDatacenters](/agency/88676092/ETDatacenters "ETDatacenters") * Published On Oct 24, 2026 at 07:56 AM IST * [![Google Preference icon](https://img.etb2bimg.com/files/cp/6e49a4e9b325074f01a6.png)](https://www.google.com/preferences/source?q=datacenters.economictimes.indiatimes.com "Select ETDatacenters as Preferred Choice on Google") Select ETDatacenters as Preferred Choice on Google ## Highlights * AI workloads cause rapid power fluctuations, challenging traditional data centre designs. * Rack power densities are increasing to hundreds of kilowatts, exceeding traditional infrastructure limits. * Peak efficiency metrics are misleading for AI, which operates more often at partial, less efficient loads. * Data centres are adopting 800V DC distribution and flat-load efficiency for AI power delivery. Artificial intelligence (AI) workloads are forcing data centres to reconsider long-standing assumptions about power delivery and efficiency. The deployment of large [GPU clusters](/tag/gpu+clusters), such as NVIDIA’s 72-GPU Vera Rubin model, is increasing rack power densities from tens to hundreds of kilowatts, with some designs projected to exceed one megawatt per rack. These [AI workloads](/tag/ai+workloads) behave differently from conventional applications, causing rapid utilization fluctuations from approximately 30 per cent to full in milliseconds during training cycles. This dynamic behaviour challenges traditional power architectures optimized for stable workloads. ### Rethinking Power Efficiency Historically, power conversion systems focused on peak efficiency, or the maximum efficiency achieved at a specific operating point. However, AI workloads rarely operate in a steady-state, spending more time at partial loads where efficiency often declines. Even a one- or two-percentage-point drop in efficiency can lead to substantial energy losses across hundreds or thousands of GPU racks. This inefficiency increases heat generation, cooling requirements, and operational costs. ### High-Voltage Distribution and Flat-Load Efficiency Traditional 48-54V DC busbar architectures struggle to scale with increasing rack power requirements. Lower voltages demand higher currents for the same power, leading to resistive losses, larger cabling needs, and increased material costs, such as 200 kilograms of copper for a 1MW rack. Data centre operators are now considering two strategies: adopting higher-voltage power distribution architectures, such as ±400V or [800V DC](/tag/800v+dc) models, and maintaining flatter efficiency profiles across the full operating range. Higher voltages reduce current, copper requirements, and resistive losses, supporting greater rack densities. Flat-load efficiency ensures consistently high performance across the fluctuating load ranges typical of AI workloads. This approach helps reduce energy losses, lower heat generation, and improve the predictability and scalability of power systems. Philip Zuk, senior vice president and general manager, AI and Datacenter, with [OmniOn Power](/tag/omnion+power), states that these combined approaches help design power systems for how AI actually behaves. ## Comments ![Comment](/_icons/images/et-default-user.svg) What are your thoughts?

These [AI workloads](/tag/ai+workloads) behave differently from conventional applications, causing rapid utilization fluctuations from approximately 30 per cent to full in milliseconds during training cycles. This dynamic behaviour challenges traditional power architectures optimized for stable workloads. ### Rethinking Power Efficiency Historically, power conversion systems focused on peak efficiency, or the maximum efficiency achieved at a specific operating point. However, AI workloads rarely operate in a steady-state, spending more time at partial loads where efficiency often declines. Even a one- or two-percentage-point drop in efficiency can lead to substantial energy losses across hundreds or thousands of GPU racks. This inefficiency increases heat generation, cooling requirements, and operational costs. ### High-Voltage Distribution and Flat-Load Efficiency Traditional 48-54V DC busbar architectures struggle to scale with increasing rack power requirements. Lower voltages demand higher currents for the same power, leading to resistive losses, larger cabling needs, and increased material costs, such as 200 kilograms of copper for a 1MW rack. Data centre operators are now considering two strategies: adopting higher-voltage power distribution architectures, such as ±400V or [800V DC](/tag/800v+dc) models, and maintaining flatter efficiency profiles across the full operating range. Higher voltages reduce current, copper requirements, and resistive losses, supporting greater rack densities. Flat-load efficiency ensures consistently high performance across the fluctuating load ranges typical of AI workloads. This approach helps reduce energy losses, lower heat generation, and improve the predictability and scalability of power systems. Philip Zuk, senior vice president and general manager, AI and Datacenter, with [OmniOn Power](/tag/omnion+power), states that these combined approaches help design power systems for how AI actually behaves. ## Comments ![Comment](/_icons/images/et-default-user.svg) What are your thoughts?

Forecast Trend Report by Period ![Loading Indicator](/images/loading/Indicator.png)![Loading Indicator](/images/loading/Indicator-dark.png) ![Photo: Shutterstock](https://media.bloomingbit.io/news/91ac9640-57f9-48ed-8127-5690736c1ec0.webp?w=800) *Photo: Shutterstock* SpaceX is struggling to raise $40 billion to build out artificial intelligence infrastructure, Bloomberg reported, as rising borrowing costs complicate the effort amid growing investor concern over AI spending. Bloomberg reported on October 24 that SpaceX is seeking to raise $40 billion in debt through a special purpose vehicle, or SPV, to finance purchases of Nvidia AI chips. The company has had difficulty reaching agreement on the financing terms. The transaction is structured so SpaceX would not assume the debt directly. By raising the funds through an SPV, the company aims to reduce the burden on its balance sheet and preserve an investment-grade credit rating. Goldman Sachs and other financial firms are negotiating terms with investors including Apollo Global Management. Those talks have become more difficult as concern grows over the large debt loads building up across AI companies, making it harder to finalize details such as interest rates. In recent weeks, negotiations included discussion of some subordinated debt at yields in the mid-8% range, Bloomberg reported. Investors are now reassessing the financing terms as volatility in financial markets increases. SpaceX's existing debt burden is also a variable. Its credit rating is near speculative grade, fueling concern that additional borrowing could add pressure to that rating. Still, SpaceX plans to continue pursuing the financing. Chief Financial Officer Bret Johnson said in a recent earnings release that he is confident the company can raise funds prudently while maintaining an investment-grade credit rating. Infra & Chips.content: * [United States](/news/us) * / * [Electronic Equipment and Components](/news/us/electronic-equipment-components) * / * NYSE:APH # How Investors Are Reacting To Amphenol (APH) Strong Q3 Growth Expectations [Simply Wall St](/news/about-simply-wall-st-news) Reviewed by[Sasha Jovanovic](/news/about-simply-wall-st-news/sasha-jovanovic) * Amphenol is heading into its third quarter 2026 earnings release with analysts expecting significant year over year increases in revenue and earnings, supported by strong demand in automotive, industrial and AI focused IT datacom end markets. * The business enters this reporting date with IT datacom already at 43% of Q2 2026 sales and a positive Earnings ESP paired with a favorable Zacks Rank. This highlights how much of the current story rests on AI infrastructure and broader segment breadth. * We will now look at how Amphenol's upbeat Q3 earnings expectations around AI related IT datacom could reshape its investment narrative. Spot opportunities across the AI hardware supply chain by scanning our hand picked [55 AI infrastructure stocks](https://simplywall.st/discover/investing-ideas/473744/ai-infrastructure-stocks/global), which echoes Amphenol's exposure to datacenter and connectivity build outs. Advertisement ## Amphenol Investment Narrative Recap To own Amphenol, you need to believe the company can keep turning its broad connector portfolio into steady demand across AI heavy IT datacom, automotive, industrial, defense and aerospace. The latest commentary keeps that story intact, with IT datacom already 43% of sales and AI focused projects shaping near term momentum. The key near term swing factor is whether AI related IT datacom orders and broader end markets stay strong enough to absorb any pockets of weakness, such as the softer communications networks activity management has flagged. The biggest risk remains that AI driven growth cools while higher taxes and debt costs weigh on earnings power. The most relevant data point today is Amphenol’s upcoming Q3 2026 report on October 28, where analysts expect a significant year over year step up in revenue and EPS across Communications Solutions and Harsh Environment Solutions. That print will effectively test the current narrative around AI infrastructure and content gains in vehicles and industrial gear. A positive surprise would reinforce the idea that recent double digit organic growth and higher margins seen in earlier quarters are feeding through consistently, including from areas like IT datacom and the CommScope CCS acquisition. Any shortfall, or a weaker tone on AI data center demand or tax headwinds, would quickly refocus attention on valuation sensitivity and the company’s higher debt load. ## Analyst Assumptions Behind the Amphenol Story Analysts are effectively asking you to look several years ahead with Amphenol and weigh up a sharper earnings profile against today’s rich set up. They are building models around revenue that rises by 20.5% a year over the next three years, paired with profit margins that move from 17.7% today to 21.5% by 2029. On their numbers, earnings today of US$5.1b are projected to reach US$10.9b in 2029, with some forecasts stretching as high as US$12.2b. That path assumes not only healthy AI focused IT datacom demand but also that acquisitions and end markets like industrial, defense and automotive keep supporting higher returns on a larger base. Those same models bake in modest dilution, with the share count expected to grow by 0.73% per year for the next three years. The projected outcome is then discounted back using a 9.05% rate in the Simply Wall St work. This is one way to translate longer dated cash flows into a number investors can compare with the current Amphenol share price. Amphenol's narrative projects US$50.8b revenue and US$10.9b earnings by 2029. This builds on 20.5% yearly revenue growth and a roughly US$5.8b earnings increase from US$5.1b today.
